source.title: AbsTopK: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders For Bidirectional Features
source.authors: Xudong Zhu; M. Khalili; Zhihui Zhu

page_placements.theme: Antipodal concepts and sign: splitting into two non-negative latents

record.tranche_reason: The study compares SAE activation constraints and reports a controlled example of one feature encoding opposite concepts. This bears on whether SAE objectives can produce or reduce feature fragmentation, but it does not test dictionary-size splitting.
record.gate_note: The study does not sweep dictionary size or test whether larger features partition a smaller feature's inputs. Figure 1 reports a controlled man/woman example for one AbsTopK feature. Table 2 separately reports transformed feature-absorption scores; that benchmark does not test the specified parent/child takeover pattern. Other steering, probing, and reconstruction results do not directly measure the claim's splitting behavior.
record.test_reason: Table 2 reports the SAEBench first-letter absorption metric, which follows Chanin et al.'s method. It is reported for TopK, JumpReLU and AbsTopK SAEs on four LLMs and two layers each. That measures V4's parent-fails/child-takes-over absorption in a new setting: other architectures and models. Absorption stays non-zero everywhere. The paper's central bidirectional-feature result (Figure 1) concerns a different construct and fits no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that non-negativity in ReLU/JumpReLU/TopK SAEs fragments bipolar concepts, and that AbsTopK lets single features encode them. They add that AbsTopK improves reconstruction and most SAEBench probing/steering scores, and that it matches or beats Difference-in-Means on the HarmBench/MMLU steering trade-off.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes AbsTopK, an SAE with hard thresholding over largest-magnitude activations, and compares it with TopK and JumpReLU. It does not reproduce a dictionary-size splitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The controlled example tests a man/woman contrast; SAE architecture and model layer vary in the absorption benchmark, whose results vary across those conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: An AbsTopK feature activates positively for 'man' and negatively for 'woman' on controlled minimal pairs. The authors argue that non-negativity forces conventional SAEs to split such antipodal concepts into two atoms.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-negative SAE activations split bidirectional (antipodal) concepts into separate unidirectional latents; signed activations let one latent encode both poles.

record.problems: The directly relevant bidirectional example is one qualitative feature on controlled sentence pairs; its model and layer are not stated. The study does not compare dictionary sizes or test input partitioning, nested families, or model-native feature units. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported absorption scores.
record.rows_left_out: Other results in Tables 1 and 2, Figures 2–4, and the probing and steering sections are not rows because they report reconstruction, capability, or task scores rather than dictionary-size splitting or the controlled bidirectional-feature result.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size sweep. Expansion factor is fixed at 16.
No size-dependent splitting and no open SAE releases; all SAEs are self-trained.
No nested families or concept hierarchy measured.
Effect of changing SAE size or sparsity on absorption is not tested. Absorption is reported at one width and one k per model; only architecture varies.
No cross-size latent decomposition or novel-latent analysis.
No test of splitting on correlated or hierarchical inputs, and no Matryoshka SAEs. The non-negativity argument concerns antipodal pairs, not coarse-to-fine splitting.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The absorption metric follows SAEBench/Chanin et al. Table 2 reports 1 − absorption, so raw absorption is 1 − value. The appendix describes absorption loosely ('starts with S' absorbed into 'short'), but cites the standard first-letter procedure. The Gemma layer is listed as 14 in Table 2 but 16 in Appendix B. The bidirectional example is a single qualitative feature, with no comparison showing how TopK splits the same pair.

versions.untested_parts: No increase in dictionary size, coarse-to-fine replacement, input coverage partition, or directional proximity is tested.
Training SAEs on four LLMs is not a test of size-dependent splitting across large models or open SAE releases.
No nested feature families or hierarchy of concepts is measured.
The first-letter absorption benchmark does not test whether a parent fails to fire where a specific child takes over, or whether size or sparsity changes that pattern.
No larger-to-smaller latent decomposition, novel-latent count, or completeness of a dictionary is measured.

The study examines a non-negativity constraint and AbsTopK on a controlled contrastive example, but does not test correlated or hierarchical input structure, Matryoshka SAEs, or whether SAE features correspond to the model's own units.

relationships.reason: Raw absorption stays about 0.20–0.53 in every cell. Changing architecture (including allowing negative activations) shifts it by at most ~0.07 and never removes it (r2–r25). No uncertainty is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Raw absorption stayed around 0.20–0.53 in every model and layer. Switching architecture, including allowing negative activations, shifted it by at most about 0.07 and never removed it; no uncertainty is reported.

relation.reason: Absorption is measured for every model, layer and architecture, though it is a side benchmark and the paper does not vary width or sparsity for it.

tranche.reason: The paper runs the SAEBench first-letter absorption metric (Chanin method) on new architectures and models. It is a side benchmark in a paper about a new SAE variant, so T3 (new setting with a result on the claim) fits.

source_check.notes: All 25 Table 2 values match. The table is in Appendix E (the main text calls it Table 3) and reports absorption as 1 - original. Gemma is labelled L14 in Table 2, but the setup, Table 1 and Fig. 4 use 12/16. One width (16x), no uncertainty. The text is the arXiv v2 preprint (Oct 2025) and states no venue.

statements.correction: arXiv:2510.00404 layers: Pythia-70M 3, 4; GPT2-small 6, 8; Gemma2-2B 12 and 14 (Table 2; setup lists 16); Qwen3-4B 18, 20. Raw absorption (1 - reported score) runs from 0.20 (Qwen3-4B L20 AbsTopK) to 0.53 (Pythia-70M L3 TopK). Expansion factor 16 for all; fixed k only for TopK/AbsTopK, JumpReLU uses the prior-work config.
statements.problem: The 0.20-0.53 range and 16x width are right, but the conditions say 'layers 6-20'. This study's Pythia-70M SAEs are at layers 3 and 4, and they supply the top of the range (0.53 = Pythia L3 TopK).

statements.correction: Raw absorption: AbsTopK is lower than TopK in 6 of 8 model-layer cells (by 0.02-0.07), equal at GPT2 L8 (0.33), and higher at Gemma L12 (0.27 vs 0.24). Max shift 0.07 (Pythia L3), never zero. No uncertainty reported.
Qwen3-4B AbsTopK absorption scores 0.79 (L18) and 0.80 (L20), raw 0.21 and 0.20; reported as 1 - original.
GPT2-small raw absorption L6: AbsTopK 0.34, TopK 0.37, JumpReLU 0.35; L8: 0.33 for all three. TopK/AbsTopK k=76; JumpReLU uses the prior-work config; 16x expansion.
statements.problem: The ~0.07 maximum comes from Pythia-70M L3. On GPT2-small the three architectures differ by at most 0.03 raw (none at L8). Also, the GPT2-small TopK/JumpReLU values are in the record (r15, r16, r18, r19), and fixed k applies only to TopK/AbsTopK.

statements.correction: Max raw difference among the three architectures is 0.07 (Pythia L3: AbsTopK 0.46 vs TopK 0.53).
AbsTopK raw: Pythia L3/L4 0.46/0.47; Gemma2-2B L12/L14 (setup says 16) 0.27/0.30; Qwen3-4B L18/L20 0.21/0.20.
Pythia-70M and Qwen3-4B (also GPT2-small, Gemma2-2B) show non-zero first-letter absorption for TopK/JumpReLU/AbsTopK SAEs (raw 0.20-0.53).

Figure 1: SAE feature 15741 positive on man, negative on woman, on one-token-differing sentence pairs. The authors say non-negative SAEs either fragment such concepts into separate bases or discard one direction.
